title: Exits from gold ETFs top $100 billion for 2026, even as inflows remain net positive - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
Exits from physically-backed gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for this year topped a record $100 billion last week, while investments continue to be net positive.

Data from the World Gold Council showed that for every dollar invested last week, there was an outflow of $3. Overall, investments in ETFs last week were $1.18 billion, while redemptions were $3.34 billion, leaving inflows net negative at $2.15 billion.

Year-to-date (YTD) redemption crossed a record $100 billion. The record outflow registered so far is $78.27 billion in 2025. With seven weeks to go, exits are already about 30 per cent higher. Investments at $140 billion may not top last year’s record inflows of $167.18 billion.

Gold ETF investors began exiting soon after the Iran war broke out. The pace has gathered over the past few weeks, with investors in the UK and China, who had stayed invested for a major part of the year, redeeming.

Darshan Desai, CEO of Aspect Bullion & Refinery, said gold witnessed a sharp correction over the past week, with the sell-off driven by a stronger dollar, rising bond yields and expectations of tighter monetary policy by the US Federal Reserve.

Prithviraj Kothari, Managing Director at RiddiSiddhi Bullions, and President of India Bullion and Jewellers Association, said gold had a brutal week as investors raised cash. Hawkish Fed minutes, a 97 per cent chance of a December rate hike, 10-year yields above 5.1 per cent and a dollar near a 19-month high all weighed on prices.

“A selloff in AI stocks set off margin-driven selling, and Iran tensions gave no support,” he said.

Renisha Chainani, chief research officer at Augmont, said US Fed rates set the tone all week. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting showed that nearly every policymaker expects more tightening to bring inflation back towards 2 per cent.

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said October’s pause was about the pace of hikes, not their direction. By Friday, CME FedWatch was pricing a roughly 97 per cent chance of a 25 basis points hike at the December 8-9 meeting, she said.

Last week, redemptions were led by investors in the US, who encashed $1.35 billion. Outflows from China were $417 million, the UK - $342 million, Switzerland - $220 million and Japan - $127.8 million. Data on Indian ETFs were not available.

Net positive YTD inflows in China and the UK dropped below $10 billion last week to $9.79 billion and $9.64 billion, respectively. Indian investments are assessed at $5 billion, while in the US, they were $2.9 billion, lower than Switzerland’s $3.45 billion. Investments in Germany were positive at $2.63 billion, in France $1.07 billion and in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region $1.04 billion.

Jateen Trivedi, VP Research Analyst - Commodity and Currency, LKP Securities, said the stronger dollar continues to remain a major headwind for bullion and could restrict further gains. “Going ahead, market focus will remain on key US economic releases, particularly the PCE Price Index and GDP data, which could provide fresh cues on inflation, economic growth and the Fed’s future interest-rate trajectory,” he said.

Volatility is likely to remain elevated amid dollar movements and global economic developments.

“Thanksgiving (November 26) cuts the week short, so volumes will be thin and price swings could be sharp in either direction. After a 9.5 per cent weekly fall, gold looks oversold on momentum indicators, so a short-covering bounce is possible,” said Chainani.

A lasting recovery, however, will probably need one of three things: a pause in the dollar’s rally, a softer November CPI print on December 10, or a clear signal from Fed Chair Warsh that the hiking cycle is nearly over, she said.

On Monday, gold increased by nearly 2.5 per cent to $3,616 an ounce at 1815 hours IST. The yellow metal has plunged by over 35 per cent after soaring to a record high of $5,608 on January 29, 2026.

A stronger dollar, higher Treasury yields and hopes of higher US Fed rates due to surging inflation dragged gold this year, mainly after the Iran war broke out on February 28. Higher crude oil prices, too, impacted the precious metal.

Between 2024 and January 2026, the yellow metal soared on hopes of US Fed rate cuts, geopolitical tensions and the trade war between the US and its other global partners.
